newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy fails to break Israel-PLO deadlock.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy fails to break Israel-PLO deadlock.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's Middle East peace envoy said he was going home on Monday, having failed to achieve a breakthrough in Israeli-PLO talks on Hebron after 15 days of trying.

As veteran mediator Dennis Ross pulled up stakes, French President Jacques Chirac pitched his tent for three days of talks in Israel and Palestinian-ruled areas aimed at making Europe a co-sponsor of peace moves.

Israel and the PLO have been trying to hammer out a deal on a long-promised Israeli troop pullback from Hebron, the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank cities due to be handed over to Palestinian rule in a 1995 accord.

"There were hopes that we could finalise in some areas. That didn't materialise," said Ross, dispatched by Clinton after violence erupted. He said talks, though continuing, were so specific that his involvement was less important.
The two sides, who last week said they were on the verge of closing a deal, said problems had arisen. Israeli leaders accused the Palestinians of unspecified delaying tactics.

"Maybe someone reasons that it's possible to stretch out this matter for several days in order to create some sort of atmosphere and pressure against Israel. This doesn't help," Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told Israel Television.

PLO security official Mohammad Dahlan said there was still no agreement on such major security issues as Israel's demand for a right of hot pursuit into areas due to be handed over to Palestinian police.
A senior Israeli government source said there was disagreement on one significant but unspecified security issue.
Palestinians and Israelis both insisted Ross's departure did not signify a crisis. A diplomatic source suggested Ross wanted to leave early to avoid devaluing his influence in the slow-moving talks.

Violence that claimed the lives of 60 Arabs and 15 Israelis in September prompted Clinton to call a White House summit attended by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and to send Ross to the region.
Clinton had made Middle East peace talks a centrepiece of his foreign policy, and administration officials had hoped for a breakthrough with U.S. elections only two weeks away.

The Hebron handover has been held up since March by Islamic suicide bombings and Netanyahu's concern for the security of 400 Jews living and studying in enclaves in the heart of the West Bank city among 100,000 Arabs.
A PLO official said Washington would continue to be represented in the talks by U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and U.S. Consul-General in East Jerusalem Edward Abington.
Chirac, taking Europe's drive for a Middle East peacemaking role to a reluctant Israel, told young Israelis on Monday that only a Palestinian state could guarantee them real security.

In a policy speech to technology students in the northern city of Haifa, Chirac said: "A recognised Palestinian state will provide Israel with a true partner. Only such a partner will be capable of making, and adhering to the commitments that are necessary for the security of Israel."
Netanyahu won election in May pledging "peace with security" but rejecting any further territorial concessions to the Arabs. He brands a Palestinian state a mortal danger to Israel.
A defiant junior French minister visited PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem on Monday, lending support to Palestinian claims to the holy city which Israel calls its eternal capital.
Chirac sent junior health minister Herve Gaymard to the PLO's Orient House headquarters after Israel refused to let Foreign Minister Herve de Charette make the trip.

"The meaning of my visit here today is...to say that as long as permanent settlement of the Palestinian question has not been achieved, the status quo applies concerning the status of Jerusalem," Gaymard said.

Israel captured Arab East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it in a move the international community refused to recognise. The PLO regards East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
